newsitem.title: PERU: Chronology of Peru's seven-week-old hostage crisis.
newsitem.headline: Chronology of Peru's seven-week-old hostage crisis.

text.p: The Marxist rebels of Peru's Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) stormed the Japanese ambassador's residence in Lima seven weeks ago, taking more than 500 hostages.
Here is a chronology of the main events:

TUESDAY, Dec. 17 - About 15 heavily armed rebels swarm into the diplomatic home and capture hundreds, including government officials and foreign diplomats, attending a reception. The rebels release all the roughly 80 women and some elderly men in the hours soon after the attack.
WEDNESDAY, Dec. 18 - The rebels threaten to kill their hostages unless the government frees up to 500 jailed comrades.
THURSDAY, Dec. 19 - Four ambassadors are released to be a "communications channel" between the rebels and the government.
FRIDAY, Dec. 20 - Rebels free 38 hostages.
SATURDAY, Dec. 21 - President Alberto Fujimori says he will study a non-violent "way out" if the rebels lay down their arms and free all hostages.
SUNDAY, Dec. 22 - The guerrillas release 225 hostages not linked to the government.
TUESDAY, Dec. 24 - Rebels release Uruguay's ambassador after his country frees two MRTA prisoners.
WEDNESDAY, Dec. 25 - A Japanese diplomat is released for medical reasons.
THURSDAY, Dec. 26 - An explosion is heard at the residence. Later the Guatemalan ambassador is freed.
SATURDAY, Dec. 28 - Government negotiator Domingo Palermo enters the residence for face-to-face negotiations with the MRTA. The rebels release 20 hostages.
TUESDAY, Dec. 31 - Cameramen enter building and interview rebel leader Nestor Cerpa Cartolini. Later the Honduran ambassador and an Argentine diplomat are freed.
WEDNESDAY, Jan. 1 - Rebels release seven captives, lowering hostage total to 74.
TUESDAY, Jan. 7 - A rebel fires two gunshots into the air in the early hours.
FRIDAY, Jan. 10 - Rebels fire four shots into the air in the early hours. Palermo arranges a second meeting with Cerpa.

SUNDAY, Jan. 12 - Planned meeting between Palermo and Cerpa is called off as rebels insist the talks centre on the release of jailed MRTA members. Palermo proposes a "guarantor commission" made up of the government, MRTA, Red Cross and the Vatican's representative, Peruvian Roman Catholic bishop Juan Luis Cipriani.
MONDAY, Jan. 13 - Rebels fire three bursts of gunfire into air during daylight.
WEDNESDAY, Jan. 15 - Rebels accept government idea of "guarantor" commission and suggest additional representation from Guatemala and a European country.
THURSDAY, Jan. 16 - Government rejects idea of Guatemala as "guarantor" and announces visits to MRTA jailed comrades by relatives or the Red Cross are banned.
FRIDAY, Jan. 17 - Rebels free an anti-terrorist police chief on medical grounds. Government and rebels agree on Canadian ambassador as a member of the guarantor commission.
TUESDAY, Jan. 21 - Police taunt rebels by approaching residence and throwing stones over the wall into the compound.
WEDNESDAY, Jan. 22 - Rebels respond to police provocation with shots fired into the air in the early hours. Police helicopter makes series of fly-pasts above residence.
THURSDAY, Jan. 23 - Fujimori visits neighbouring Bolivia and vows to wipe out MRTA rebels in region after crisis.
FRIDAY, Jan. 24 - Police send armoured cars rumbling past the occupied residence.
SATURDAY, Jan. 25 - Rebels fire two warning shots into the air mid-afternoon.
SUNDAY, Jan. 26 - Rebels free an ill police chief on medical gounds.
MONDAY, Jan. 27 - Rebels fire several gunsots at police making lewd gestures as they pass the residence in a parade of armoured vehicles.
WEDNESDAY, Jan. 29 - Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto and Fujimori agree to meet in Toronto to discuss crisis after Tokyo's criticism of police tactics.
SATURDAY, Feb. 1 - Fujimori and Hashimoto agree to push for direct talks with rebels and appoint Japan's ambassador to Mexico, Terusuke Tarada, as observer at such negotiations.
MONDAY, Feb. 3 - U.S. President Bill Clinton meets Fujimori in Washington and applauds his handling of the crisis.

The 72 remaining hostages include Japanese and Bolivian ambassadors, Fujimori's brother Pedro, top Peruvian government and security force officials, and about two dozen Japanese diplomats and businessmen.
